title: Joiner edits relationship details and gets an unexplained failure
preconditions: A created the space; B joined as the partner.
B opens Account and chooses Edit relationship.
B changes the anniversary date and saves.

actions.note: B opens Edit relationship and saves a new date.

expected_behavior: A non-creator is either not offered the edit action or told plainly that only the creator can change space details.
A failed save explains the rule and preserves the current values.
The UI never implies that the partner's change was saved.
candidate_failure_modes: The partner taps a working-looking Edit relationship row, fills the form, and receives only "Unable to save. Please try again."
The partner retries because the message implies a transient network problem.
The partner believes the anniversary date changed when the server rejected it.

observed_code_behavior: Spaces enforce one active membership per user and one active partner per space at the storage layer.
Joining redeems an invite once; an expired or already-redeemed code is rejected, and a historical partner slot is permanently bound.
Leaving flips the caller's membership to left and keeps shared history for the remaining member.
Space hydration, foreground refresh, and mutation callbacks are scoped to the signed-in user id.

hypothetical_user_behavior: A fictional participant (Iris Vale) said: "We are auditing Aoi for things that do not need to exist. Walk through the shared-memory flow you actually used this week: the composer, the Keep button, pending rows, retry and edit, author labels, the feed and gallery, empty and failed states, and every confirmation or helper line. For each one, ask out loud: "Why does this even exist?" Then say what would break if it were removed, and what it cost you. Name the three most useless things and the one thing you would keep. Do not propose a redesign; remove."

A fictional participant (Iris Vale) said: "Three I'd delete without a eulogy:

1. The Keep button. The composer already holds what I typed — "Keep" is a second act of consent for something I already committed to. It splits one intention into two taps and implies the first tap was provisional.

2. Pending rows as a *separate visual state*. If the write is optimistic, render the real row with a quiet sync glyph. A ghost list teaches me a new vocabulary (pending/failed/retry) for a problem I didn't know I had.

3. The confirmation line after every action. "Saved!" is the interface applauding itself. The row appearing *is* the confirmation. Same for the helper text under empty states that explains a flow before I've asked for it — that's a spec doc in a costume.

Runner-up: the retry + edit pair on failed writes. One action, two buttons, and neither tells me whether my text survived.

What I'd keep: author labels. Not because they're pretty, but because attribution is the only metadata here that changes how I read the content. Everything else is chrome.

Cost of all of the above: a beat of "did it work?" latency on a gesture that should be frictionless. And with reduced motion on, the pending fade is the *only* feedback left — so the decorative layer is load-bearing. That's the tell."
Iris Vale assumes: the interface should teach itself
Iris Vale assumes: empty states should be designed
Oren Pike assumes: a saved item survives relaunch
Oren Pike assumes: an error is not a dead end
